blocks.hero.subhead: OCD can make you feel trapped by thoughts you don't want and rituals you can't stop. Exposure and response prevention (ERP) helps you take your life back, one step at a time.
blocks.request.heading: You don't have to keep living by OCD's rules

signs.items.text: Unwanted thoughts keep coming back, and they scare you.
You check, wash, count, or repeat things until it feels "just right."
You mentally review, pray, or seek reassurance over and over.
You worry you've done something wrong, even when you know you haven't.
The rituals take up more and more of your day.
You've researched OCD and thought, "That's it."

blocks.faith.heading: When OCD shows up in your faith
blocks.faith.body:
For some people, OCD attaches to faith: fear of having sinned, of offending God, or of not believing "enough," with compulsions like repeated confession, prayer, or reassurance seeking. This is sometimes called scrupulosity. Your counselor understands how OCD can show up in faith, and can help you tell the difference between OCD and your convictions.

Faith-based work here never means more reassurance or more rituals. It means learning to rest in grace instead of certainty.

If you'd rather leave faith out, your counselor's care is just as thorough, and they follow your lead. [How faith works at Freedom](/christian-counseling)

sections.body: OCD is a cycle of obsessions (unwanted, distressing thoughts, images, or urges) and compulsions (things you do, or think, to make the distress go away). Compulsions bring relief for a moment, but they teach your brain the thought was dangerous, so it comes back stronger. Some people's compulsions are mostly mental, sometimes called "Pure O." It's common, it has a name, and it can be treated.
sections.heading: OCD isn't about being neat

sections.body: OCD can latch onto almost anything: germs, harm, sex, relationships, faith, your body, getting things "just right." Many people search for their exact fear online, can't find it, and decide it must be something other than OCD. It usually isn't. Whatever the content, OCD runs on the same loop: an unwanted thought, a surge of distress, and something you do or think to make it go away. That's why treatment targets the loop, not the theme, and why there's no kind of OCD we don't work with.
sections.heading: The theme isn't the problem. The process is.

sections.body:
ERP is the most studied therapy for OCD. With your counselor, you build a list of situations that trigger your OCD, from easiest to hardest. Then, step by step, you practice facing them without doing the compulsion. Over time, your brain learns the thought isn't an emergency, and the urge to ritualize fades.

You're never forced into anything. You and your counselor choose each step together, and acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) skills help you make room for discomfort along the way. Afraid to start? Read [What is ERP therapy?](/what-is-erp-therapy-a-gentler-look-for-anyone-afraid-to-start)

Your counselor may also use the Brain Lock approach, a four-step way to recognize an OCD thought for what it is, step back from it, and turn your attention to something that matters.
sections.heading: Exposure and response prevention, at a pace you choose

sections.body:
Here's the part most people don't expect: compulsions are your mind's way of calming the obsession. They work for a moment, and that's exactly why OCD keeps coming back stronger. So the goal isn't to make the thought go away. It's to let it be there without doing the compulsion, and to keep doing something that matters to you while the discomfort passes. Things that help in the moment:

- **Notice and name it.** "That's an OCD thought." Labeling it puts a little space between you and it.
- **Slow your breathing.** Try a physiological sigh (two quick breaths in through the nose, one long breath out) or box breathing (in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4).
- **Relax your body.** Tense and release one muscle group at a time.
- **Change your temperature.** Splash cold water on your face, or take a cold shower.
- **Change your surroundings.** Go for a walk.

Then turn back toward what you were doing, without the ritual. Your counselor will help you practice this until it gets easier.

blocks.expect.heading: Your first session
blocks.expect.body: Your first session is about understanding your OCD: what the thoughts are, what you do in response, and how it's affecting your life. You won't be asked to face anything before you're ready. Sessions are in our Middletown office or online.
